      <h1 class="proj-title">Which Capacity Matters Most for Earned Revenue? Evidence from U.S. Nonprofit Performing Arts Organizations</h1>
      <p class="proj-desc">What began as a Chicago-focused independent study grew into a national panel data analysis — starting with in-depth interviews with 5 local theater organizations, then expanding to examine how human, programmatic, and financial capacity shape earned revenue among 1,864 U.S. nonprofit performing arts organizations (2019–2024).</p>
    </div>

      <h2 class="section-title">Project timeline</h2>
      <div class="timeline">
        <div class="tl-item">

          <p class="tl-date">Oct – Nov 2025</p>
          <p class="tl-title">Exploratory interviews</p>
          <p class="tl-desc">Conducted in-depth interviews with 5 Chicago nonprofit theater organizations to identify structural constraints on earned-revenue generation and financial sustainability.</p>
        </div>

          <div class="tl-dot tl-done"></div>
          <p class="tl-date">December 2025</p>
          <p class="tl-title">Independent Study Report</p>
          <p class="tl-desc">Cross-sectional analysis of 69 Chicago theaters — examining revenue structure types, deficit ratios, and operational characteristics. Supervised by Professor Yasen Peyankov, University of Illinois Chicago.</p>
        </div>

          <p class="tl-date">Spring 2026</p>
          <p class="tl-title">Expanded to national scale</p>
          <p class="tl-desc">Extended the quantitative analysis to 1,864 U.S. nonprofit performing arts organizations using SMU DataArts national panel data (2019–2024) and a two-way fixed effects model.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tl-item">
          <div class="tl-dot tl-done"></div>

          <img src="aaae-conference.jpg" alt="AAAE Conference Presentation" style="width:100%; max-width:400px; border-radius:8px; margin-top:8px;">
        </div>
        <div class="tl-item">
          <div class="tl-dot tl-done"></div>
          <p class="tl-date">June 2026</p>
          <p class="tl-title">Full paper completed</p>
          <p class="tl-desc">Completed the full academic paper with two-way fixed effects regression, robustness checks, and policy implications.</p>
        </div>

    </div>

    <div class="proj-section">
      <h2 class="section-title">Key findings</h2>
      <ul class="finding-list">
        <li class="finding-item">
          <div class="finding-icon fi-teal">
            <i class="ti ti-users" aria-hidden="true"></i>
          </div>
          <p class="finding-text"><strong>Human capacity is the strongest predictor of earned revenue.</strong> A one-standard-deviation increase in workforce size is associated with a 5.1 percentage point increase in the earned revenue ratio (β = 0.048, p &lt; .001) — the largest effect among the three capacity dimensions.</p>
        </li>
        <li class="finding-item">
          <div class="finding-icon fi-blue">
            <i class="ti ti-theater" aria-hidden="true"></i>
          </div>
          <p class="finding-text"><strong>Programmatic capacity also matters, but less so.</strong> A one-standard-deviation increase in program occurrences is associated with a 3.8 percentage point increase in the earned revenue ratio (β = 0.022, p &lt; .001). A Wald test confirms human capacity has a significantly stronger association than programmatic capacity (z = 5.52, p &lt; .001).</p>
        </li>
        <li class="finding-item">
          <div class="finding-icon fi-amber">
            <i class="ti ti-alert-triangle" aria-hidden="true"></i>
          </div>
          <p class="finding-text"><strong>Financial capacity shows a negative association — consistent with the starvation cycle.</strong> Higher months of cash on hand is associated with a lower earned revenue ratio (β = −0.004, p &lt; .001), suggesting organizations with greater reserves may be holding rather than deploying financial slack toward earned revenue generation.</p>
        </li>
        <li class="finding-item">
          <div class="finding-icon fi-gray">
            <i class="ti ti-check" aria-hidden="true"></i>
          </div>
          <p class="finding-text"><strong>Findings are robust across multiple specifications.</strong> The direction and significance of all three capacity dimensions hold when excluding pandemic years (2020–2021), controlling for organizational scale, and using log earned revenue as an alternative dependent variable.</p>
        </li>
      </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="proj-section">
      <h2 class="section-title">Implications</h2>
      <p class="body-text">The findings suggest that capacity dimensions matter unequally for earned revenue generation — and that cultural policy should reflect this hierarchy rather than treating capacity support as an undifferentiated goal.</p>
      <ul class="finding-list">
        <li class="finding-item">
          <div class="finding-icon fi-teal">
            <i class="ti ti-users" aria-hidden="true"></i>
          </div>
          <p class="finding-text"><strong>Prioritize human capacity investment.</strong> Because workforce size shows the strongest association with earned revenue, funding structures that support staffing — such as general operating support and multi-year funding — may be more effective than project-based grants that leave personnel costs uncovered.</p>
        </li>
        <li class="finding-item">
          <div class="finding-icon fi-blue">
            <i class="ti ti-theater" aria-hidden="true"></i>
          </div>
          <p class="finding-text"><strong>Consider program composition, not just volume.</strong> The weaker association of programmatic capacity suggests that the balance between fee-based and free programming may matter as much as the number of programs delivered.</p>
        </li>
        <li class="finding-item">
          <div class="finding-icon fi-amber">
            <i class="ti ti-refresh" aria-hidden="true"></i>
          </div>
          <p class="finding-text"><strong>Rethink financial health indicators.</strong> High cash reserves do not predict stronger earned revenue — raising questions about whether standard financial health metrics capture what actually enables long-term sustainability.</p>
        </li>
      </ul>
      <div class="highlight-box">Capacity dimensions matter unequally — and cultural policy should reflect this hierarchy, shifting from undifferentiated capacity support toward investment in the dimensions most closely linked to earned revenue.</div>
    </div>

  </div>
</div>
